sentences.text: Harpactognathus is considered one of the largest known non-pterodactyloid pterosaurs, with an estimated wingspan of 2.5 meters and a skull length of 280 to 300 millimeters.
The definitive fossil is a rostrum measuring 130 mm in length and 42.5 mm in width, implying a total skull length of 280 to 300 mm, while an assigned humerus measures 110.5 mm in length.
This animal had an extremely broad snout that was wider than it was tall in life, containing four pairs of teeth, which distinguishes it from related genera that had fewer sets.
The only confirmed fossil of Harpactognathus is an incomplete rostrum found in 1996 at the Bone Cabin Quarry, recovered near Bone Cabin Quarry in 1996.
The genus Harpactognathus was described by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues in 2003, and the species name gentryii honors Joe Gentry, a volunteer for the Western Paleontological Laboratories.
A pterosaur mandible was discovered in 1999 within a meter of the original rostrum find.

Based on its teeth and environment, Harpactognathus was likely a terrestrial carnivore living near freshwater, unlike its piscivorous relatives; however, as a rhamphorhynchid, it may also have been an aerial predator of small prey, with recent publications suggesting scaphognathines like Harpactognathus likely lacked specializations for eating fish and were probably terrestrial predators of small vertebrates or generalists.

A premaxillary crest on the skull may have been supported by soft tissues for sexual display or represented sexual dimorphism, and Carpenter et al. (2003) presumed the function of the crest was for display purposes.

Harpactognathus was originally classified in the subfamily Scaphognathinae within the family Rhamphorhynchidae, and Harpactognathus belongs to the family Rhamphorhynchidae, but its exact position within that family remains debated.

Some researchers suggest Harpactognathus belongs to the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae rather than Scaphognathinae based on similarities to Sericipterus and Angustinaripterus, and a 2010 phylogenetic analysis by Andres, Clark, and Xu placed Harpactognathus in the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae as a close relative of Angustinaripterus and Sericipterus.

Many traits once considered unique to Harpactognathus are now recognized as also belonging to Sericipterus and/or Angustinaripterus, and it is debated whether Harpactognathus belongs to the tribe Angustinaripterini, as it was excluded from a 2022 analysis due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil.

Harpactognathus lived during the Late Jurassic period in the Morrison Formation of Albany County, Wyoming, USA, and it was found in the Salt Wash Member (Kimmeridgian stage), with the time range for Harpactognathus being from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian (152.21 to 145.06 million years ago).
It is debated whether the mandible found near the holotype actually belongs to Harpactognathus due to its slender nature and alveoli anatomy.
